lessons.title: Implementing Square Foot Gardening
lessons.body: Square Foot Gardening (SFG) divides your bed into 30cm x 30cm squares. For a 1-hectare plot, you won't use SFG everywhere, but it's perfect for high-value crops like lettuce, spinach, carrots, and onions. Build raised beds 1.2m wide and 20cm deep so you can reach the centre from both sides. Fill with a mix of 1/3 compost, 1/3 topsoil, and 1/3 sand or rice husks for drainage. In each square, plant a specific number of seeds: 16 carrots, 9 spinach, 4 lettuce, 1 tomato, or 1 pepper. Use a stick or string to mark the grid. Water gently with a watering can to avoid washing seeds away. In Africa, SFG works well in both dry and rainy seasons because raised beds drain excess water and retain moisture in dry spells. You can add a simple shade net during extreme heat. For a 10m x 10m area, you can have 80 squares, producing up to 80 lettuce heads every 8 weeks. That's 10 heads per week for a family, with surplus for sale. Start small: build 4 beds of 1.2m x 2.4m (8 squares each). Plant fast crops like radish and rocket first to see results. Keep a notebook of what you plant and when. SFG reduces weeds, saves water, and doubles yields compared to row planting. For profit, focus on crops that fetch high prices: lettuce, spinach, coriander, and spring onions. Sell to local restaurants, hotels, or neighbors. With consistent care, you can earn $50-$100 per month from just 10 squares. Remember to replant immediately after harvest to keep the bed productive. Use organic compost from kitchen waste and animal manure to keep costs low. This method is ideal for women's groups and youth because it requires little land and minimal tools.

lessons.title: Using Intercropping and Companion Planting
lessons.body: Intercropping means growing two or more crops together in the same field. Companion planting is a type of intercropping where crops help each other. For example, maize and beans: beans fix nitrogen from the air into the soil, feeding the maize. Plant maize 75cm apart, then beans 30cm apart between the maize rows. This gives you two harvests from one plot. Another classic: cabbage and onions. Onions repel cabbage pests like aphids and diamondback moths. Plant one onion between every four cabbages. In Africa, we also use 'push-pull' with Desmodium and Napier grass to control stem borers in maize. For vegetables, try carrots and spring onions: the onion smell masks the carrot fly. Or lettuce and radish: radish grows fast and can be harvested before lettuce needs the space. Legumes like cowpeas, groundnuts, and beans are excellent companions because they add nitrogen. Avoid planting tomatoes with potatoes (both get blight) or onions with beans (onions stunt bean growth). A good intercrop for profit: plant tomatoes with basil. Basil improves tomato flavour and repels whiteflies. Plant one basil between every two tomato plants. Another: spinach and strawberriesâspinach shades the soil, keeping strawberries cool. When intercropping, ensure each crop gets enough sunlight and water. Use a spacing that allows air movement to prevent fungal diseases. For a 1-hectare plot, you can divide into strips: 1m of maize, 1m of beans, alternating. This makes harvesting easier. Intercropping increases total yield by 20-40% and reduces pest damage. It also spreads your risk: if one crop fails, the other survives. For market, you can sell multiple products at once. Start with simple pairs like maize-beans or cabbage-onion. Keep records of which combinations work best in your area. Share seeds and knowledge with neighbours. This method is low-cost and uses natural processes to boost production.

lessons.title: Vertical Growing for Space Efficiency
lessons.body: Vertical growing means using poles, strings, nets, or trellises to grow plants upwards instead of letting them spread on the ground. This saves space and reduces disease because leaves don't touch wet soil. For a 1-hectare plot, you can grow many more plants by going vertical. Tomatoes, cucumbers, beans, peas, and even some squash can be trained to climb. Use wooden poles, bamboo, or metal rods. For tomatoes, drive a 2m pole into the ground next to each plant and tie the stem loosely with soft cloth or banana fibre as it grows. For beans and peas, create a teepee with three or four poles tied at the top. Plant 4-6 seeds around each pole. For cucumbers, use a strong net or wire mesh between two posts. The net should be at least 1.5m high. Plant cucumbers 30cm apart along the base. Vertical growing increases yield per square metre by 2-3 times. For example, 1 square metre of ground can hold 1 tomato plant, but with vertical training, you can harvest 5-8kg of tomatoes from that plant instead of 2-3kg. It also makes harvesting easier and reduces fruit rot. In dry areas, vertical gardens can be shaded with a cloth on the sunny side. For profit, grow high-value crops like cherry tomatoes, snow peas, and climbing beans. Sell them in small packs to supermarkets or restaurants. You can also use old plastic containers or sacks filled with soil and hung on walls or fences. Just make sure they get enough waterâvertical gardens dry out faster. Water daily, and add mulch on top of the soil. A simple trellis made from local materials costs almost nothing. Train your plants early by gently tying them when they are young. Prune side shoots of tomatoes to direct energy upward. With vertical growing, you can turn a small backyard into a productive farm. Even on a 10m x 10m plot, you can grow 50 tomato plants vertically and earn $200 per season.

lessons.title: Optimizing Plant Spacing for Yield
lessons.body: Plant spacing is the distance between plants and between rows. Correct spacing gives each plant enough sunlight, water, and nutrients. Too close, and plants compete, leading to small harvests and disease. Too far, and you waste land. For intensive planting, you want the closest spacing that still allows good growth. For leafy greens like spinach and lettuce, space plants 15-20cm apart in all directions. For carrots, thin to 5-8cm apart. For onions, 10cm. For tomatoes, 45-60cm between plants and 60-90cm between rows. For maize, 75cm between rows and 25-30cm between plants. For beans, 30-45cm between rows and 10-15cm between plants. These are general guidelines; adjust based on your soil fertility and water availability. In poor soil, give more space. In rich soil, you can plant closer. Use a measuring stick or string to mark spacing. For a 1-hectare plot, you can calculate the number of plants: area divided by (plant spacing x row spacing). For example, tomatoes at 60cm x 60cm: 10,000 mÂ² / (0.6m x 0.6m) = 27,777 plants. But you won't plant the whole hectare with tomatoes. For a 10m x 10m plot, you can fit 278 tomato plants at that spacing. If you plant closer, say 45cm x 45cm, you get 493 plants, but each may yield less. Test different spacings on small plots. Keep records of yield per plant and total yield. Often, closer spacing gives higher total yield per hectare even if individual plants are smaller. For example, maize at 75cm x 25cm gives 53,333 plants per hectare; at 75cm x 50cm, only 26,666 plants. The closer spacing usually yields more total grain if water and nutrients are sufficient. For vegetables, closer spacing works well for small crops like radish, but not for large crops like cabbage (needs 45-60cm). Always ensure air can move between plants to reduce fungal diseases. Mulch between plants to conserve water and suppress weeds. With good spacing, you can increase your harvest by 30-50% without extra land.

lessons.title: Transplanting vs. Direct Sowing Strategies
lessons.body: Transplanting means starting seeds in a nursery and moving young plants to the field. Direct sowing means planting seeds straight into the ground. Each has advantages. Transplanting is best for crops with expensive seeds (tomatoes, peppers, eggplant), slow-growing crops (cabbage, kale), or crops that need a head start (onions). It also lets you select strong seedlings and avoid gaps. Direct sowing is best for fast-growing crops (radish, spinach, carrots, beans, maize) and root crops that don't like being moved (carrots, beetroot). In Africa, transplanting helps you manage water: you can water a small nursery easily, then transplant when rains come. For a 1-hectare plot, you can raise seedlings in trays or a nursery bed. Use a fine soil mix: 1 part compost, 1 part sand, 1 part topsoil. Sow seeds thinly and cover with a thin layer of soil. Water daily with a fine rose. For tomatoes, transplant when seedlings have 4-6 true leaves, about 3-4 weeks after sowing. Harden them off by reducing water and exposing them to sun for a few days before transplanting. Transplant in the evening or on a cloudy day to reduce shock. Water immediately after. For direct sowing, prepare a fine seedbed. Sow seeds at the right depth: small seeds like lettuce 0.5cm deep, larger seeds like beans 3-5cm deep. Space seeds according to the final spacing, then thin later. Thinning is removing extra plants so the remaining ones have space. For carrots, thin to 5cm apart when plants are 5cm tall. For maize, thin to one plant per station. Direct sowing saves labour and avoids transplant shock, but you use more seeds and water. Transplanting gives earlier harvests by 2-3 weeks, which can mean higher prices at market. For profit, use transplanting for high-value crops like tomatoes and peppers, and direct sowing for bulk crops like maize and beans. Keep a nursery diary to track sowing and transplanting dates. With good planning, you can have a continuous supply of vegetables for sale.

lessons.title: Managing Microclimates within the Hectare
lessons.body: A microclimate is a small area with different conditions from the surrounding land. On your 1-hectare plot, you can create and use microclimates to grow more crops. For example, a south-facing slope gets more sun and is warmer; a north-facing slope is cooler. A wall or fence stores heat during the day and releases it at night, protecting plants from frost. In hot, dry areas, you can create shade using trees, shade nets, or tall crops like maize. Plant sensitive crops like lettuce on the shady side of maize. In cool, highland areas, use walls or stones to reflect heat onto crops like tomatoes and peppers. You can also use mulches to keep soil cool and moist. For a 1-hectare plot, map your microclimates: note where water collects after rain (drier or wetter spots), where wind hits hardest, and where the sun rises and sets. Use this map to place crops. For example, plant drought-tolerant crops like sorghum or millet on dry, windy spots. Plant water-loving crops like spinach and cabbage in low, moist areas. You can also create microclimates: dig a small trench and fill with compost to hold water, or build a low stone wall to protect from wind. In Africa, many farmers use 'zai' pitsâsmall planting holes that catch waterâto create moist microclimates in dry areas. For vegetables, use raised beds in wet areas and sunken beds in dry areas. Shade nets (50% shade) can reduce temperature by 5-10Â°C, allowing you to grow lettuce in hot lowlands. Windbreaks of vetiver grass or sisal reduce wind damage and evaporation. A simple microclimate trick: plant tall crops like maize or sunflowers on the western side to shade afternoon sun from sensitive crops. Also, use reflective mulch (silver plastic) to deter aphids and increase light. By managing microclimates, you can extend your growing season and grow crops that normally wouldn't survive. This increases your total production and profit. Keep a simple notebook of what works where. Share your findings with neighbours. Microclimate management is free and uses what you already haveâsun, wind, water, and land shape.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Intensive Planting Techniques for the One-Hectare Vegetable Enterprise

Intensive planting is not about cramming more seed into the ground. It is a business decision: every square metre of your hectare must earn its keep. On a well-run one-hectare vegetable unit in Africa â whether in Kiambu, Kenya; Mbeya, Tanzania; or Nsukka, Nigeria â intensive techniques can lift gross margin per hectare by 30â60% over conventional row planting, mainly by raising marketable yield per mÂ², shortening turnaround time to cash, and reducing input waste. This Practical Reference gives you the numbers, methods, and checklists to implement six core techniques: square foot gardening, intercropping and companion planting, vertical growing, spacing optimisation, transplanting vs. direct sowing, and microclimate management.

1. Square Foot Gardening (SFG): The Grid Discipline

Square foot gardening divides a bed into 30 cm Ã 30 cm (1 ft Ã 1 ft) squares, each planted with a fixed number of a given crop. It is ideal for high-value leafy and root vegetables where labour is available for close management. The classic planting densities are well documented: 1 per square for large plants (tomato, pepper, cabbage), 4 per square for medium plants (lettuce, basil, marigold), 9 per square for small plants (spinach, bush beans), and 16 per square for very small plants (carrots, radish, onions).

For a commercial hectare, convert open field to 1.2 m-wide raised beds with 30 cm paths â this gives roughly 6,600 mÂ² of productive bed area (about 66% of the hectare), or 7,300 squares. At 4 lettuce per square and 3 cycles per year, that is over 87,000 heads per hectare per year, versus roughly 40,000â50,000 in conventional 30 cm Ã 30 cm single-row spacing. The business case rests on seed cost, labour for thinning, and market price per head.

2. Intercropping and Companion Planting

Intercropping is a risk-management and revenue-stacking tool. Legume intercrops (beans, cowpea, groundnut) fix nitrogen and can supply 40â80 kg N/ha to the following crop, reducing fertiliser bills. Companion planting â for example, maize + beans + pumpkin (the "three sisters"), or cabbage + marigold for nematode suppression â also reduces pest pressure, cutting pesticide spend. The table below summarises proven African-relevant combinations.

Table 1. Proven intercrop and companion combinations for one-hectare African vegetable systems
Main crop Companion / intercrop Spacing (main) Key benefit Yield impact (main crop)
MaizeBeans (climbing)75 Ã 30 cmN fixation, weed suppressionâ5 to +10%
CabbageMarigold (Tagetes)60 Ã 45 cmNematode suppression0 to +15%
TomatoBasil / onion60 Ã 60 cmThrips & pest deterrence+5 to +20%
KaleLettuce45 Ã 45 cmGround cover, quick cash0 to +5%
Sweet potatoCowpea90 Ã 30 cmN fixation, soil coverâ5 to +5%

Sources: FAO (2011), Save and Grow; IITA (2018), Maize-Legume Intercropping Systems in Sub-Saharan Africa; CIMMYT (2019), Conservation Agriculture for Smallholders.

3. Vertical Growing for Space Efficiency

Vertical growing multiplies effective planting area without expanding the footprint. On a one-hectare unit, trellising tomatoes, cucumbers, and climbing beans on 2 m stakes or A-frames can raise in-row plant density by 60â100% and improve airflow, reducing fungal disease. Vertical systems also improve spray coverage and ease harvest labour, which directly affects cost per kg. For leafy crops, multi-tier vertical racks (3â4 tiers) are viable in peri-urban tunnels where land rent is high. Typical yield uplift: tomato +40â70% per mÂ² of ground; cucumber +50â80%; climbing beans +30â50%.

4. Optimising Plant Spacing for Yield

Spacing is a yield-versus-quality trade-off. Closer spacing raises total yield per hectare but reduces individual fruit size and can increase disease. The table below gives practical commercial spacings for common African vegetables.

Table 2. Recommended commercial spacings and expected plant populations per hectare
Crop Spacing (cm) Plants/ha Typical marketable yield (t/ha) Notes
Tomato (staked)60 Ã 4537,00040â60Use vertical support
Cabbage60 Ã 4537,00050â70Hybrids respond to close spacing
Onion15 Ã 10660,00025â35Direct sow or transplant
Kale45 Ã 4549,00030â45Harvest 6â8 months
Carrot20 Ã 51,000,00025â40Thin to avoid forked roots
French beans50 Ã 10200,00010â15Climbing types need trellis

Sources: AVRDCâThe World Vegetable Center (2016), Vegetable Production Training Manual; KALRO (2020), Horticulture Production Guidelines for Kenya; FAO (2019), Good Agricultural Practices for Vegetables.

5. Transplanting vs. Direct Sowing

Transplanting gives you a head start of 3â4 weeks, better crop uniformity, and lower seed cost for expensive hybrids. Direct sowing saves labour and avoids transplant shock, and is preferred for root crops (carrot, radish, beetroot) and fast leafy greens. The decision is financial: transplanting adds nursery cost (trays, media, labour) but can raise early-season price by 20â40% because you reach market when supply is low. On a one-hectare unit, a simple 10 m Ã 1 m nursery can raise enough seedlings for 0.5â1 ha of transplanted vegetables.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Pesticide and Nursery Handling

Always wear gloves, a long-sleeved shirt, and a face mask when mixing or spraying pesticides (including botanicals such as neem or pyrethrum). Never spray against the wind, never eat or drink during spraying, and observe the pre-harvest interval (PHI) on the label â typically 7â14 days for vegetables. Store agrochemicals in a locked, labelled cabinet away from food and children. In nurseries, sterilise trays and media to prevent damping-off (Pythium, Rhizoctonia), which can wipe out an entire seedling batch and delay your market window. If you feel dizzy, stop immediately and seek medical help.

6. Managing Microclimates within the Hectare

Your hectare is not uniform. Slopes, shade from trees, wind direction, and soil depth create microclimates that change yield by 20â50%. Map them:

  • Windward edges: plant windbreaks (napier grass, moringa, grevillea) to protect leafy crops.
  • Low-lying areas: frost and waterlogging risk â use raised beds or plant late-season crops.
  • Shaded zones: grow lettuce, spinach, and herbs that bolt in full sun.
  • Full-sun zones: tomato, pepper, okra, and maize.
  • Near water source: high-value, water-demanding crops (tomato, cucumber).

Mulching (straw, grass, plastic) reduces soil temperature by 3â6Â°C and evaporation by 30â50%, extending the growing window and cutting irrigation cost â a direct margin gain.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Map your hectare into microclimate zones before planting; mark sun, shade, wind, and water access.
  2. Convert at least 60% of the hectare to 1.2 m raised beds with 30 cm paths for intensive planting.
  3. Use square foot grid densities (1, 4, 9, 16 per square) for high-value leafy and root crops.
  4. Intercrop with legumes (beans, cowpea) to cut nitrogen fertiliser cost by 30â50%.
  5. Trellis all climbing crops (tomato, cucumber, beans) to raise density 40â80% per mÂ².
  6. Transplant expensive hybrids; direct sow root crops and fast leafy greens.
  7. Apply mulch to reduce irrigation and weeding labour by 30% or more.
  8. Keep a spray log, observe PHI, and wear full PPE every time.

Further Reading (free official resources)

  • FAO â Save and Grow: Sustainable Intensification of Smallholder Crop Production
  • AVRDCâThe World Vegetable Center â Vegetable Production Training Manuals
  • KALRO â Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organisation (crop guides)
  • IITA â International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (intercropping research)
  • CIMMYT â Conservation Agriculture and Sustainable Intensification resources

Prepared for RISE AFRICA Skills â Course: Maximise 1 Hectare: Vegetables for Profit. Module: Intensive Planting Techniques. All figures are indicative; validate against local market prices, input costs, and extension advice before committing capital.

quiz.q: In Square Foot Gardening, how many carrot seeds do you plant in one 30cm x 30cm square?
quiz.explanation: Carrots are small and can be planted 16 per square foot (30cm x 30cm).

quiz.q: What is the ideal width for a raised bed in Square Foot Gardening so you can reach the centre?
quiz.explanation: A width of 1.2m allows you to reach the middle from both sides without stepping on the bed.

quiz.q: Which crop is a good companion for cabbage to repel pests?
quiz.explanation: Onions repel cabbage pests like aphids and diamondback moths.

quiz.q: In maize-bean intercropping, what benefit do beans provide to maize?
quiz.explanation: Beans fix nitrogen from the air into the soil, which feeds the maize.

quiz.q: Which crop should you avoid planting with tomatoes because both get blight?
quiz.explanation: Tomatoes and potatoes are both susceptible to blight and should not be planted together.

quiz.q: What is a typical spacing for tomato plants in intensive planting?
quiz.explanation: Tomatoes need 45-60cm between plants and 60-90cm between rows for good air circulation and growth.

quiz.q: How many tomato plants can you fit in a 10m x 10m plot at 60cm x 60cm spacing?
quiz.explanation: Area = 100 mÂ², spacing = 0.6m x 0.6m = 0.36 mÂ² per plant, so 100 / 0.36 â 278 plants.

quiz.q: Which crop is best for direct sowing rather than transplanting?
quiz.explanation: Carrots have a taproot and do not transplant well; they should be direct sown.

quiz.q: When should you transplant tomato seedlings from the nursery?
options: B) When they have 4-6 true leaves
quiz.explanation: Tomatoes are ready to transplant when they have 4-6 true leaves, about 3-4 weeks after sowing.

quiz.q: What is 'hardening off' in transplanting?
options: B) Exposing seedlings to outdoor conditions gradually
quiz.explanation: Hardening off means gradually exposing seedlings to sun and wind to reduce transplant shock.

quiz.q: What is a microclimate?
options: B) A small area with different conditions from surroundings
quiz.explanation: A microclimate is a small area with distinct conditions, such as a shaded spot or a warm wall.

quiz.q: How can you create a cooler microclimate for lettuce in a hot area?
options: A) Plant on a south-facing slope
B) Use shade nets or plant on the shady side of tall crops
quiz.explanation: Shade nets or shade from tall crops reduce temperature and protect lettuce from heat.

quiz.q: What are 'zai' pits used for?
options: B) Catching and holding water for plants in dry areas
quiz.explanation: Zai pits are small planting holes that capture rainwater and create moist microclimates.

quiz.q: Which of these is a benefit of vertical growing?
options: B) Reduced disease from soil contact
quiz.explanation: Vertical growing saves space, reduces soil-borne diseases, and makes harvesting easier.

quiz.q: What is a good support for climbing beans?
options: D) A rope on the ground
quiz.explanation: A teepee made of three or four poles tied at the top provides a sturdy support for climbing beans.

quiz.q: How much can vertical growing increase yield per square metre for tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: Vertical training can increase tomato yield per square metre by 2-3 times compared to ground sprawl.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for maize in a monocrop?
quiz.explanation: Maize is typically spaced 75cm between rows and 25-30cm between plants.

quiz.q: Why is closer spacing often better for total yield per hectare?
options: B) More plants per area, even if individual plants are smaller
quiz.explanation: Closer spacing increases the number of plants per hectare, which can raise total yield if resources are sufficient.

quiz.q: What is a disadvantage of transplanting?
options: B) Requires more labour and care
quiz.explanation: Transplanting requires a nursery, daily care, and careful handling, which is more labour-intensive.

quiz.q: Which crop is best to intercrop with maize to control stem borers?
quiz.explanation: Desmodium (push-pull technology) repels stem borers and is intercropped with maize.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of thinning in direct sowing?
options: B) To give remaining plants enough space
quiz.explanation: Thinning removes excess plants so the remaining ones have adequate space, light, and nutrients.

quiz.q: How deep should you sow lettuce seeds?
quiz.explanation: Lettuce seeds are small and should be sown very shallow, about 0.5cm deep.

quiz.q: What is a good microclimate for tomatoes in a cool highland area?
options: B) Near a wall that reflects heat
quiz.explanation: A wall stores heat during the day and releases it at night, protecting tomatoes from cold.

quiz.q: Which mulch can deter aphids and increase light reflection?
quiz.explanation: Silver reflective mulch repels aphids and reflects light onto plants, improving growth.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of transplanting for profit?
options: B) Earlier harvest and higher prices
quiz.explanation: Transplanting gives earlier harvests by 2-3 weeks, which can fetch higher market prices.

quiz.q: In Square Foot Gardening, how many lettuce plants per square?
quiz.explanation: Lettuce is spaced 4 per square foot (30cm x 30cm) in SFG.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good companion for tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: Basil improves tomato flavour and repels whiteflies.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for carrots after thinning?
quiz.explanation: Carrots should be thinned to 5-8cm apart to allow roots to develop properly.

quiz.q: How can you create a moist microclimate in a dry area?
options: B) Dig sunken beds or zai pits
quiz.explanation: Sunken beds and zai pits catch and hold water, creating moist microclimates for plants.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of intercropping for pest management?
options: B) Confuses pests and reduces damage
quiz.explanation: Intercropping with pest-repellent plants can confuse or repel pests, reducing crop damage.
